Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to Plato, Protagoras 345e and files it under Socratic School. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Socrates

Socrates (c. 470/469–399 BCE) was an Athenian citizen who wrote nothing and yet redirected Greek philosophy from cosmology toward ethics and the care of the soul.

How to read this passage

Moral philosophy asks whether morality is objective, how reasons bind us, and how character, rules, and consequences relate. Traditions differ on whether duty, virtue, or outcomes come first. This passage enters that discussion through morality, knowledge, will.

Concepts in this quote

Morality
Morality in philosophy concerns right and wrong, obligation, and the standards by which we judge persons and acts.
Knowledge
Knowledge is the philosophical study of what we can justifiably claim to know—and where certainty ends.
Will
Will appears in this archive as a live philosophical concern—not a slogan. These verified English passages show how thinkers treat will as a problem of judgment, practice, or explanation.
